draft.title: Planning for audience and purpose
card: Audience
the people who will read or hear the text. Their age, interests and what they already know decide the words and tone you choose.
Purpose
what the text is meant to do, such as inform, persuade, entertain or explain. Knowing this tells you what to include and what to leave out.
Form
the type of text that suits the audience and purpose, such as a speech, a news article, a letter or a short story. Each form has its own features.

Then sort your ideas into a logical order, such as the order events happen or from the strongest point to the weakest. A short plan, like a list or mind map, helps you do this before you start writing.
draft.remember: Decide who you are writing for, what the text must do and which form fits. Then put your ideas in order.

a.q: Mia is about to write a speech. Why should she decide on her audience before she starts?
opts: It helps her choose suitable words, tone and content
It lets her skip the step of putting ideas in order
It means she can use the same form for every task
It makes the proofreading stage unnecessary later
a.why: Knowing who will listen helps Mia choose words, tone and ideas that suit them. The other options are wrong because the audience does not remove the need to order ideas or to check the text later.
a.clue: Think about who will be listening to her.

b.q: Jack's class wants Year 7 students to join a new lunchtime chess club. Jack plans a poster. Which choice best matches his purpose?
opts: Persuade Year 7 students to come along to the club
Entertain readers with a story about a chess game
Inform historians about where chess began
Explain to teachers how to mark a chess test
b.why: The club needs new members, so the poster must persuade Year 7 students to join. The story option is tempting because a poster can be fun, but entertaining readers is not what the text must do here.
b.clue: What does the club want its readers to do?

a.best: It helps her choose suitable words, tone and content

b.best: Persuade Year 7 students to come along to the club

problems.detail: The right option is the only one that repeats 'Year 7 students' from the question, and it is the longest. The other options name unrelated audiences (teachers, historians), so a student could pick it by matching words without understanding purpose.
